item.title: The impact of α3β4 partial agonist AT-1001 on oxycodone withdrawal
item.description:
Purpose: Opioid withdrawal remains a major barrier to successful treatment of opioid use disorder. Non-opioid treatments such as clonidine and lofexidine reduce acute somatic symptoms but do not address affective and protracted withdrawal signs. Neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), particularly the α3β4⁎ subtype, are a promising alternative target implicated in opioid withdrawal. Here we investigated whether AT-1001, a high-affinity α3β4⁎ partial agonist, reduces somatic and affective signs of oxycodone withdrawal in mice.

Experimental approach: Male and female C57BL/6J mice were rendered dependent on oxycodone (60mg/kg/day) or vehicle (0.9% saline) via a 7-day osmotic minipump infusion. Twenty-four hours after minipump removal, mice received an acute subcutaneous injection of vehicle, lofexidine (0.5mg/kg), or AT-1001 (0.3, 0.9, or 3mg/kg), followed by assessment of somatic withdrawal signs. In a separate cohort of oxycodone-dependent mice, animals received the highest dose of AT-1001 or lofexidine and were assessed two weeks post-minipump removal for mechanical sensitivity and anxiety-like behaviors (light/dark box assay).

Key results: Our results showed that AT-1001 dose-dependently reduced somatic withdrawal signs in oxycodone-treated mice. In contrast to lofexidine, AT-1001 attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity and anxiety-like behavior compared to the vehicle group in oxycodone-dependent mice. Furthermore, AT-1001 had no significant effect on oxycodone-induced antinociception, as evaluated in the warm-water immersion assay.

Conclusion and implications: . Our findings suggest that AT-1001 effectively reduces oxycodone withdrawal signs without altering its antinociceptive effects. This supports α3β4⁎ partial agonists as promising candidates for further development as a safer and more comprehensive opioid withdrawal treatment.

Contreras KM, Palamar A, Buzzi B, Oros A, Buttar B, Damaj M

item.title: Safety and efficacy of psilocybin-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder: Open-label extension of a phase II randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Psilocybin-assisted therapy (PAT) has shown promise for alcohol use disorder (AUD) in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). It remains unknown, however, whether patients derive additional benefit when psilocybin is administered open-label after completion of blinded treatment. Here, we report safety and efficacy outcomes from an open-label extension of a Phase II RCT of PAT for AUD (NCT02061293).

Methods: Fifty-nine adults with AUD received a single open-label administration of psilocybin (25-40mg/70kg) accompanied by four hours of manualized therapy. During the preceding double-blind phase, 29 of these participants had received psilocybin (psilocybin-psilocybin group; PP) and 30 had received the active placebo diphenhydramine (diphenhydramine-psilocybin group; DP). Mixed-effects models for repeated measures evaluated alcohol consumption (percent heavy drinking days [PHDD], drinks per day [DpD], and percent drinking days [PDD]), alcohol craving, abstinence self-efficacy, and treatment readiness across a four-month follow-up.

Results: Psilocybin was well tolerated, and no serious adverse events occurred. Among participants with higher drinking intensity at extension entry, decreases in PHDD, DpD, and PDD were observed at Month 1 but returned to entry levels thereafter. Craving, abstinence self-efficacy, and treatment readiness improved in both PP and DP groups one week after administration, with variable trajectories thereafter.

Discussion: After completion of the double-blind trial, a single open-label psilocybin administration was associated with maintained remission among most participants who entered abstinent and with acute but largely transient reductions among those who were still drinking heavily. Whether the limited durability reflects the lower intensity of extension treatment, the relative treatment resistance of residual drinking, differences in motivation, or other design-related factors cannot be determined from these data.

Clinical trial registration: NCT02061293, A Double-Blind Trial of Psilocybin-Assisted Treatment of Alcohol Dependence, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02061293.

Pagni BA, Ross S, Mennenga S, Bhatt S, Zeifman RJ, Petridis PD

item.title: Neighborhood violence, visible drug activity, and substance use among urban youth: Mental health and community factors
item.description:
Background: Adolescent substance use and exposure to neighborhood violence frequently co-occur in U.S. urban settings, particularly among racially minoritized and low-income youth. Despite shared exposure to environmental risk, some adolescents report low to no substance use. Guided by the adverse community experiences and resilience framework, this study identified classes of neighborhood risk and substance use among urban adolescents and examined whether emotional, behavioral, community, and demographic factors differentiated profile membership.

Methods: Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 743 adolescents aged 13-21 residing in a large Northeastern U.S. city. Five dichotomous indicators (witnessed neighborhood violence, seen drugs sold in their neighborhood, and lifetime vaping, alcohol, and marijuana use) were analyzed using latent class analysis. Multinomial logistic regression examined associations between class membership and emotional, behavioral, community, and demographic factors.

Results: A three-class solution was retained: No Neighborhood Risk Exposure/Low or No Substance Use (34%), High Exposure/Low or No Use (40%), and High Exposure/Polysubstance Use (26%). Compared with the High Exposure/Low or No Use class, the No Neighborhood Risk Exposure/Low or No Use class reported higher neighborhood support and lower racial discrimination, missing school, and suicidal thoughts. The High Exposure/Polysubstance Use class differed from the High Exposure/Low or No Use class primarily by higher depressive symptoms.

Conclusions: Low substance use should not be interpreted as low need among adolescents exposed to neighborhood risk. Adolescent health and well-being efforts should assess mental health distress, suicidal ideation, racial discrimination-related experiences, and school disengagement alongside substance use.

item.title: Prejudicial essentialist bias in cognitive neuroscience studies with people who use drugs
item.description:
Objectives: Professional judgement can be biased (or prejudiced) by the incidental social characteristics of marginalised clients. Perhaps unexpectedly, psychologists have been hypothesised to express prejudicial essentialist bias in their writing; disproportionately invoking pathological constitutional deficits to explain observed differences in study participants with marginalised social characteristics.

Methods: To test whether this bias exists in cognitive neuroscience publications, 67 case-controlled studies reporting lower cognitive task performance in people who use drugs (PWUD) versus controls were collated. The percentage of explanations of PWUD's performance using essentialist terms ('deficits', 'dysfunction', 'impairments') versus neutral-agnostic terms ('difference', 'change', 'alteration' etc.) were tested for associations with PWUD's social characteristics, study effect size and publication year.

Results: Deficit descriptions were used on 64% of occasions and were significantly associated with PWUD's social characteristics including their mean age (r = 0.40), percent male (r = 0.24), primary drug (η2 = 0.24), and dependence severity indexed by their recruitment from clinical sources (η2 = 0.12) and characterisation using clinical diagnostics (η2 = 0.15); but not with the effect size of the task performance difference (r = 0.029) or publication year (r = -0.18).

Conclusions: Psychologists' unwarranted causal inference that task performance differences arise from constitutional pathogenic origins may be prejudiced by the incidental social characteristics of their PWUD sample. This bias may be explained by professional incentives, journal remit and author training influencing narrative construction. Solutions for the bias may involve meta-scientific auditing, strengthening of language guidelines, and critical reflective practice implemented through positionality statements in quantitative research.

Oldfield CJ, Owens M, Hogarth L

item.title: Accuracy of self-reported e-cigarette nicotine strength in young adults (18-26) and adults (27-54) who vape and differences in their preferences for nicotine strength and flavor
item.description:
Purpose: To examine the accuracy of self-reported nicotine strength and differences in nicotine strength and flavor preferences between young adults and adults who vape. Accurate assessment of nicotine exposure is essential for understanding vaping behavior and informing public health research, yet the reliability of self-reported nicotine strength remains unclear.

Methods: We recruited 61 young adults (18-26) and 65 adults (27-54). Participants reported the nicotine strength of their vaping products (high vs. low) and provided product samples for laboratory analysis. Nicotine concentrations in the samples were measured using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Participants were asked about their preferred flavor and whether they prioritize nicotine strength or flavor when purchasing a product.

Results: The agreement between self-reported and laboratory-derived nicotine strengths (Cohen's kappa) was 0.73 for young adults and 0.71 for adults. More young adults used high-nicotine products (≥24mg/mL) than adults (50.8% vs. 30.8%; p = 0.022). Most participants in both age groups used fruit/sweet products more than non-sweet (tobacco/menthol). However, nicotine strength was more frequently identified as the primary factor influencing product choice than flavor.

Conclusion: Among young adults who vaped regularly in this sample, self-reported nicotine strength showed substantial agreement with laboratory-derived low/high nicotine-strength categories, supporting its use for broad classification in research settings. Nicotine strength appeared to be more important for young adults than flavor. This study provides novel evidence that nicotine concentration plays a central role in vaping behavior and highlights the importance of regulating nicotine strength alongside flavors to reduce vaping rates among young people.

item.title: Longitudinal pathways from prenatal alcohol exposure and infant behaviors to verbal IQ and working memory
item.description:
Objective: Assess infant behaviors as early predictors of Verbal IQ and Working Memory (V/WM) differences related to prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) from 4 to 21 years of age.

Study design: Longitudinal observational study of 387 infants (60% PAE; 48% male; 81% Black), from birth to 21 years. Verbal IQ or Working Memory was measured at 4, 9, 15, or 21yrs. with tests of intellectual functioning. Infants were administered a visual preference task and the Neurobehavioral Assessment (NB) at birth, the Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence (FTII) at 6.5 /12 mo. and Mental Development Index (MDI) of the Bayley Scales at 6.5, 12, 24 mos. Latent growth curve modeling assessed the association of PAE with V/WM over time, assessing infant behaviors as predictors.

Results: 2-year Bayley MDI (Indirect effect (IE) = -0.11, SE = 0.045; p = 0.015) was linked to both PAE and V/WM. Abnormal NB correlated with V/WM (β = -0.21, p = 0.023; β = 0.23, p = 0.047, for intercept and slope, respectively). FTII at 6.5 months correlated with MDI (β = 0.16, p = 0.007) and FTII at 1 year (β=0.17, p = 0.005). Neonatal visual preference marginally correlated with FTII at 6.5 months (β = -0.13, p = 0.097). All relationships were controlled for other prenatal exposures, the home environment, and blood lead level.

Conclusions: PAE was related to poorer Verbal IQ and WM from 4 to 21 years of age, via 2-year cognitive outcomes associated with 6- and 12-month infant mental and visual recognition performance. Neonatal neurobehavioral abnormalities were related to V/WM independent of PAE. Infant assessments could aid early identification of cognitive sequelae of PAE in high-risk populations.

Singer LT, Schultheis E, Albert JM, Kim JY, Minnes S, Min MO

item.title: Validation of a novel systematic social observation for assessing the social and built environment in neighborhoods surrounding community-based substance use programs
item.description:
Background: Systematic social observation (SSO) quantifies changes in the social and built environment and can be useful for evaluating the neighborhood effects of substance use programs.

Methods: We developed, implemented, and validated an SSO instrument in the Bronx, New York City, and Providence, Rhode Island. Research assistants assessed neighborhoods in the Bronx (4/19/2023-6/22/2023) and Providence (11/4/2024-12/20/2024) following a randomization schedule to minimize temporal biases. We used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and Bayesian multi-level item response theory (IRT) models to derive social and built environment indices and externally validated the measures against arrest data.

Results: EFA for the Bronx (n = 564) and Providence (n = 463) identified three factors assessed with the instrument: drug litter, people, and built environment. IRT-based social and built environment indices exhibited positive spatial autocorrelation (the Bronx Moran's I = 0.393, P < 0.001; Providence Moran's I = 0.068, P < 0.001). In the Bronx, item severity and discrimination were highest for the drug litter factor; item parameters were relatively uniform in Providence. The Bronx index was associated with total (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.04-1.95) and drug-related (IRR = 1.60, 95% CI = 1.10-2.32) arrests. The Providence index was not associated with arrests.

Conclusions: Our SSO protocol can be replicated in diverse settings to evaluate the neighborhood effects of substance use programs and broader effects of neighborhood conditions on substance use. The social and built environment indices for the Bronx and Providence may be useful outcomes in future studies. External validation suggests the Bronx index captured drug-related environmental variation; the Providence index may capture variation unrelated to policing patterns.

Chambers LC, Li Y, Krieger MS, Allen B, Kral AH, Goldman JE

item.title: Association between parental overdose and substance use disorder and youth overdose and SUD: A large linked commercial claims study
item.description:
Background: Youth drug overdoses (OD) and substance use disorders (SUD) are major public health concerns, yet the association between parental and offspring OD is poorly understood and has not been examined using linked insurance claims data. We examined parental OD/SUD associations with youth diagnoses and treatment utilization.

Methods: Using Merative MarketScan (2017-2024), we studied adolescents (12-17) and young adults (18-25) with a first OD or SUD diagnosis linked to parents/guardians (≥6 months enrollment). Participants were classified as Any OD or SUD-only, with OD + SUD as an Any OD subgroup. Exposure was parental OD/SUD history; secondary outcomes were naloxone, medications for opioids use disorder (MOUD), and behavioral health services within 6 months. Logistic regression adjusted for sex and region.

Results: Among 6.5 million youth, Any OD occurred in 0.5% of adolescents and 0.6% of young adults; SUD-only in 0.8% and 2.6%. Parental OD/SUD was associated with higher odds of Any OD and SUD-only in adolescents (adjusted odds ratios [AORs]: 3.6 [95% CI: 3.4 -3.9] and 3.8 [3.5 -3.9]) and young adults (3.7 [3.5 -4.0] and 3.4 [3.3 -3.5]), respectively. AORs for OD + SUD were 4.3 [3.7 -4.9] and 4.1 [3.7 -4.5], respectively. Naloxone and MOUD receipt were descriptively higher among young adults with parental OD/SUD (p < 0.0001); adolescent treatment and behavioral health utilization did not differ meaningfully by parental diagnosis.

Conclusions: Parental OD/SUD history was consistently associated with elevated odds of youth OD and SUD, with modest increases in medication receipt only among young adults. Youth from affected families may benefit from early identification and tailored interventions.

item.title: Opioid misuse and opioid use disorder by sexual identity in U.S. adults: Findings from the 2021-2022 NSDUH
item.description:
Background: Sexual minority adults experience elevated rates of substance use, yet recent national data on opioid misuse, opioid use disorder (OUD), and heroin-related perceptions by sexual identity and age remain limited.

Methods: We used pooled 2021-2022 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) data among heterosexual, gay/lesbian, and bisexual adults (n = 90,066; gay men n = 1312; bisexual men n = 1835; lesbian/gay women n = 1428; bisexual women n = 6389). Survey-weighted logistic regression models, stratified by sex and adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, estimated adjusted odds of lifetime opioid misuse, lifetime heroin use, past-year opioid misuse, past-year OUD, perceived heroin risk, and perceived heroin access by sexual identity. Age-stratified models estimated disparities in lifetime and past-year opioid misuse across adulthood.

Results: Bisexual women had more than twice the adjusted odds of all four opioid outcomes relative to heterosexual women (aORs=2.30-2.96), with disparities in opioid misuse evident across all age groups. Lesbian/gay women had elevated adjusted odds of lifetime opioid misuse and heroin use only. Bisexual men had higher adjusted odds of lifetime opioid misuse (aOR=2.02 [1.59-2.57]) and past-year opioid misuse (aOR=1.95 [1.38-2.76]); gay men had no significant adjusted disparities. Bisexual men and women had lower adjusted odds of perceiving great risk from trying heroin; bisexual women also had higher odds of perceived heroin access.

Conclusions: Sexual identity disparities in opioid misuse and OUD persist in national data, with particularly elevated prevalence among bisexual women. Bisexual adults may benefit from age-inclusive opioid screening and harm-reduction messaging responsive to their lower perceived heroin risk.

Schuler MS, Stein BD

item.title: Age and intensive care unit admissions following opioid overdose
item.description:
Background: Older adults are increasingly impacted by the opioid crisis, yet age-related differences in overdose presentation, management, and outcomes leading to intensive care unit (ICU) admission remain poorly characterized. This study examined age-related variations in drug exposures, interventions provided, and hospital utilization among patients experiencing an opioid overdose.

Methods: The Toxicology Investigators Consortium (ToxIC) Fentalog Study was conducted at 10 US medical centers and collected data on patients who presented to emergency departments with confirmed non-fatal opioid overdose, and available waste serum samples between 9/21/2020-4/14/2026 were included. Chart reviews captured presentations, treatments, and hospital utilization. Toxicologic analyses were performed at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education. Nested multivariable logistic regressions assessed whether age improved predicted ICU admission, after accounting for sociodemographic characteristics and drug classes detected.

Results: Among 1930 patients, 15.3% were admitted to the ICU, 7.8% received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and 5.8% were intubated. Length of hospital stay varied by age, with patients 65 + years old staying longest (median: 22.0h, IQR: 87.0, p < 0.001). Illicit opioids were less commonly detected in older adults (p < 0.001), while prescription opioids were more common (p < 0.001). Age cohort did not significantly predict ICU admission, although prescription benzodiazepine (AOR: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.1, 1.9) and opioid (AOR: 0.7, 95% CI: 0.5, 0.9) detection did.

Conclusions: Older age was associated with longer hospital stays but did not predict ICU admission after adjustment for relevant covariates. Benzodiazepine and opioid exposures showed a modest association with ICU utilization. Further work should clarify how pharmacologic combinations influence clinical severity across age groups.

Falise AM, Berger J, Lopez-Quintero C, Culbreth R, Aldy K, Krotulski A
